titulo: What goes to the queue (and what stays with you)
lead: Not every task should go to the queue. Before installing anything, you run your list through three questions and get a table: runs on its own, runs with a gate, or stays with you.
objetivo: Classify ten of your tasks as runs on its own, runs with a gate, or stays with you, and say where each gate goes.
hero_alt: Hands sorting paper cards into three piles on a table.

aprende.t: What should not go in the queue
Your queue on paper, with ten lines

nos.detalhe: Start with what you repeat. A task that comes up every week, with the same kind of input, is a natural candidate.

itens.sub: a link, a file, a subject
a file or text you can read

nos.detalhe: Clear input and a result you can check: it goes in the queue. If the result also goes out into the world (publishes, sends, spends credits), add a gate before that step.
Internal use and low-cost errors: if the result is poor, you just redo it. It runs all night without asking for anything.
The agent does the heavy work and stops. You read, correct, and approve. Only then does it continue to publish or spend.

itens.t: Vague input or a delicate decision

nos.detalhe: A request that needs a conversation ("make this better"), a business decision, or an irreversible action you can't review. It can go back in the queue when you know how to describe the input and the result.

secoes.legenda: Click each block. The question that changes the destination most is the third: consequences outside call for a gate.

secoes.titulo: The three questions, one at a time
secoes.sub: With examples of what runs today in inemaccbot.

texto: The queue doesn't talk with you along the way. The task needs to fit on one line: a link, a file path, or a subject.
inemaccbot skills show the format (the bot's commands stay in Portuguese): transcrever: https://…, explicativo: <subject> | vertical, imagem: a red fox in the snow | ratio=16:9.

exemplo.texto: "Give the presentation a little polish." What should be improved, and how much? Keep it with you or turn it into a concrete input.

texto: In the morning, you'll check the result. If it's a file (text, video, image), you can review it in minutes. If it's "I did several things," there's no way to tell whether it came out right.
In the bot, this is a contract: the agent finishes with RESULT: <path>, and the bot checks that the file exists and has the expected extension.
Publishing on behalf of the company, sending something to a client, spending paid credits: this is where the gate comes in. The agent prepares it and stops; you approve.
Transcribing a meeting for you to read yourself has no outside consequences. It runs on its own.

exemplo.texto: The /promoavatar writes the copy for each audience and stops. Only after you approve does it move on to the video and reel.

passos.titulo: Is it okay to start over from scratch?
texto: This question doesn't change whether it goes in the queue; it changes the type. If starting over from scratch is cheap, one skill (one step) is enough. If there's partial work you'd hate to throw away, the right choice is a flow (several phases, with state and resumption).
You'll use both in lessons 5 and 6.

blocos.rot: Ask your agent to review the table
blocos.conteudo:
Read the fila-no-papel.md file. For each row, check:
1. Does the input fit on one line (link, file, or topic)?
2. Is the result a file or text you can check?
3. Does it have outside consequences (publishing, sending, spending)? If so, is a gate marked?
Point out any rows that should have a different destination and explain why. Don't edit the file.

abas.html:
• Row 4 ("organize the calendar"): vague input. I suggest "stays with you" or rewriting it as "list this week's calendar conflicts."
  • Row 7 ("reply to client emails"): outside consequences without a gate. I suggest "queue with gate": the agent drafts, you send.
  • The others look good.

• No gates in ten rows: check that nothing is being published or sent.
  • Every row has a gate: you'll spend the morning approving things; see what is for internal use only.
  • Results like "multiple files" or "improve": hard to check.

secoes.sub: Prerequisite: steps 1 and 2 of the program.

exercicios.texto: Fill in the table with ten repetitive tasks from your work. For each one, list the input in one line, a verifiable result, the destination, and where the gate goes. Ask your agent to review it using the example above.
exercicios.pronto: All 10 rows are filled in, and at least two have a gate.

secoes.sub: The explanation appears after your answer.

perguntas.p: For which task is the human gate most important?
opcoes: Summarizing PDFs for you to read yourself.
Publishing a post on behalf of the company.
Listing the files in a folder.
perguntas.explica: Put the gate before anything with outside consequences: publishing, sending, spending. Internal use with low-cost mistakes can run on its own.

perguntas.p: Should "Make the presentation better" go in the queue?
opcoes: Not yet: the input is vague. Either keep it with you or turn it into a specific request.
Yes, as long as it uses the most expensive model.
perguntas.explica: The queue can't talk to you in the middle of the night. Without clear input, there's no way to check whether the result is right.

perguntas.p: A task has several steps, and one in the middle is expensive. If the last step fails, you don't want to start over. Which type should you use?
opcoes: A flow, which saves the state of each phase and resumes from the one that failed.
Neither: expensive tasks don't go in the queue.
perguntas.explica: A skill works when starting over from scratch is okay. When partial work is valuable, the flow saves each phase, and /refazer resumes from the one that failed.
